turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break this down simply.

Think of your choices in four main buckets:

What kind of plant?
Roses: This is our main focus. We sell premium own-root roses in 1-gallon containers with soil.
Other plants: We also have some perennials (like lavender, catmint, hydrangeas) and flower bulbs (like tulips and daffodils) at certain times of year.
Which rose shape and size? When you look at roses, you’ll see different “types.” In simple terms:
Shrub/bush roses: Round, bushy plants that are great in beds and borders. Good general choice for beginners.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need a trellis, fence, or arch. Great if you want a rose-covered structure.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low and spreading, good for the front of beds or covering an area.
Hybrid tea roses: Classic “long-stemmed” look, usually one big bloom per stem, nice for cutting.
Will it live in your climate and spot?
Hardiness zone: At the top of our website you can pick your zone. That helps you see roses that can handle your winter temperatures.
Sun: Most roses want full sun (about 6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day). Partial shade (around 4 hours) is possible for some, but sun is still important.
When and how it arrives
All our roses are shipped as live plants in 1-gallon containers with soil, not bare root.
You can choose an estimated delivery date at checkout so the plant arrives close to when you want to plant.
Roses should be planted outside (never kept indoors), either in the ground or a larger pot, around your frost dates.
Optional extras
Soil amendments (like compost or manure) help improve your soil’s structure and nutrients.
Fertilizers give your rose ongoing food to support growth and blooms.
Garden markers are metal tags or stakes you can buy to label your roses, but every rose already comes with a simple plastic name label.

To make this really practical for you: are you mainly trying to choose your very first rose variety, or are you trying to understand how to plant and care for it once you order? That will help me focus on the next steps for you.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. Here’s a simple starter checklist for a first-time rose grower:

A good spot
Sun: Aim for about 6+ hours of direct sun if you can.
Soil drainage: Roses dislike “wet feet,” so avoid spots where water sits after rain.
Basic planting supplies
Shovel and small hand trowel.
Mulch (like bark chips) to put a 2–3 inch layer on top of the soil after planting; this helps hold moisture and keep roots cool.
Helpful (optional) soil amendments These are not required, but they make getting started easier:
Bone meal: Supports strong root growth.
Cow manure: Adds long-lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost: Improves soil structure and can also be used as a gentle top layer to protect roots.
Worm castings: Add nutrients and improve soil aeration.
Fertilizer (this one really matters)
Roses do best with regular feeding.
A liquid fertilizer is especially helpful in the first year because it is easy for the plant to take up.
We offer several options (like OmniMeal and Founders Fish Fertilizer), but you can use any rose-appropriate fertilizer and follow the label directions.
Basic care know-how Once you have the plant and spot ready, having simple instructions to follow makes a huge difference:
Our main how‑to collection is here: How‑To Articles.
Two especially helpful guides:
Planting Roses (step‑by‑step planting)
Pruning (how and when to prune; pruning means cutting back canes to shape the plant and encourage new growth).

If you’d like, tell me your zip code and whether you’ll plant in the ground or in a pot, and I can give you a super short, step‑by‑step “Day 1” plan tailored to your situation.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and good on you for thinking ahead.

Here’s how to use your very first rose properly, step by step:

When it arrives
Take it out of the shipping box right away.
Keep it outdoors in a bright spot protected from harsh wind while you get the planting spot ready.
Water the soil in the pot so it is evenly moist (not soggy).
Choose the spot
Pick a place with about 6 or more hours of direct sun each day.
Avoid low spots where water puddles; roses like well‑drained soil.
Planting in the ground (simple version)
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and as deep as the pot.
Gently slide the rose out of its 1‑gallon container, keeping the soil around the roots together.
Set it in the hole so the surface of the soil from the pot is level with the surrounding ground.
Backfill with your garden soil (you can mix in compost if you have it), and press gently so there are no big air gaps.
Water deeply to settle everything.
Add a 2–3 inch layer of mulch (like bark or compost) on top, keeping it a couple of inches away from the base of the plant.
First feeding
Wait a couple of weeks after planting before using fertilizer.
Then use a gentle or liquid rose fertilizer according to the label; this “feeds” the plant without shocking it.
Early care
Keep the soil evenly moist, especially for the first few months, but not waterlogged.
Don’t worry if it doesn’t bloom a lot right away; it’s busy making roots its first season.
